title: Microservice characteristics
short: Microservices are independently deployable components aligned to business capabilities.
answer: Good boundaries consider business ownership and deployment independence. They add distributed-system complexity.
followups: Microservices vs modular monolith?
interview: Microservices are independently deployable components aligned to business capabilities.

title: API Gateway vs Load Balancer
short: A load balancer distributes traffic; a gateway also applies API-level policies.
answer: Gateways commonly handle auth, rate limits, routing and transformation.
followups: Can both coexist?
interview: A load balancer distributes traffic; a gateway also applies API-level policies.

title: Service discovery
short: It lets clients find healthy service instances without hardcoded addresses.
answer: Discovery can be client/server-side. Kubernetes commonly provides service discovery via DNS/services.
followups: Client vs server discovery?
interview: It lets clients find healthy service instances without hardcoded addresses.

title: Sync vs async communication
short: Synchronous calls wait for responses; async messaging decouples timing.
answer: Async improves buffering/decoupling but introduces eventual consistency and duplicate handling.
followups: When use Kafka?
interview: Synchronous calls wait for responses; async messaging decouples timing.

title: Saga pattern
short: A Saga coordinates local transactions with compensating business actions.
answer: Each service commits locally. Compensation is a new business action, not a distributed DB rollback.
followups: Orchestration vs choreography?
interview: A Saga coordinates local transactions with compensating business actions.

title: Outbox pattern
short: Business state and an event record are committed in one local transaction.
answer: A publisher sends outbox events later. Consumers still need idempotency.
followups: How handle duplicate publish?
interview: Business state and an event record are committed in one local transaction.

title: Idempotency
short: Repeating a request produces the same intended business result.
answer: Idempotency keys are useful for payments/order creation; persist key and outcome.
followups: Where store the key?
interview: Repeating a request produces the same intended business result.

title: Retry policy
short: Retry transient failures with bounded attempts.
answer: Use timeouts, exponential backoff and jitter. Avoid retrying non-idempotent operations without safeguards.
followups: When should you not retry?
interview: Retry transient failures with bounded attempts.

title: Bulkhead pattern
short: Bulkheads isolate resource pools so one dependency cannot consume all capacity.
answer: Separate executors, pools or concurrency limits reduce blast radius.
followups: Bulkhead vs circuit breaker?
interview: Bulkheads isolate resource pools so one dependency cannot consume all capacity.

title: Eventual consistency
short: Different services may temporarily see different state before convergence.
answer: Define acceptable stale windows and user-visible intermediate states.
followups: How handle stale reads?
interview: Different services may temporarily see different state before convergence.

title: Resilience patterns
short: Timeouts, retries, circuit breakers, bulkheads and graceful degradation control failures.
answer: Each protects a different failure mode. Combining them requires careful limits to avoid retry storms.
followups: How avoid retry storms?
interview: Timeouts, retries, circuit breakers, bulkheads and graceful degradation control failures.

title: Distributed tracing
short: Tracing follows requests across services using trace/span context.
answer: Trace is end-to-end; spans represent operations. Propagation preserves correlation.
followups: Metrics vs logs vs traces?
interview: Tracing follows requests across services using trace/span context.

title: Microservice monitoring
short: Use metrics, structured logs, traces and health signals tied to user impact.
answer: Monitor rate, errors, latency, saturation, JVM, DB pools and broker lag.
followups: What is an SLO?
interview: Use metrics, structured logs, traces and health signals tied to user impact.

title: API versioning
short: Prefer backward-compatible evolution and explicit versions for breaking changes.
answer: Additive changes and deprecation reduce consumer disruption.
followups: How deprecate consumers?
interview: Prefer backward-compatible evolution and explicit versions for breaking changes.

title: Rate limiting
short: Rate limiting controls traffic per identity/resource.
answer: Token bucket, leaky bucket and sliding windows are common; distributed systems may need shared state.
followups: Global vs per-user?
interview: Rate limiting controls traffic per identity/resource.

title: Message broker
short: A broker decouples producers and consumers and can buffer work.
answer: Kafka, RabbitMQ and cloud messaging have different ordering/delivery models.
followups: Queue vs topic?
interview: A broker decouples producers and consumers and can buffer work.

title: Kafka topic/partition/group
short: Topics hold records, partitions provide parallelism and per-partition ordering, groups divide consumption.
answer: More consumers than partitions do not increase that group's partition parallelism.
followups: What determines ordering?
interview: Topics hold records, partitions provide parallelism and per-partition ordering, groups divide consumption.

title: At-least-once vs at-most-once
short: At-least-once can duplicate; at-most-once can lose messages.
answer: Exactly-once must be considered end-to-end. Idempotent processing is often the practical target.
followups: How make consumer idempotent?
interview: At-least-once can duplicate; at-most-once can lose messages.

title: Service mesh
short: A service mesh moves service-to-service networking policies into infrastructure proxies/nodes.
answer: It can provide mTLS, routing and telemetry but adds platform complexity.
followups: When avoid a mesh?
interview: A service mesh moves service-to-service networking policies into infrastructure proxies/nodes.

title: Debug production 500
short: Preserve evidence and correlate the failure through logs, metrics and traces.
answer: Check trace ID, stack trace, deployment/config changes, downstream and DB errors before restarting.
followups: What if logs are missing?
interview: Preserve evidence and correlate the failure through logs, metrics and traces.

title: Prevent cascading failures
short: Use timeouts, bounded concurrency, circuit breakers, bulkheads and load shedding.
answer: Unlimited waiting exhausts threads/connections; isolation prevents blast radius.
followups: Load shedding vs rate limiting?
interview: Use timeouts, bounded concurrency, circuit breakers, bulkheads and load shedding.

title: Blue-green deployment
short: Run old and new environments and switch traffic after validation.
answer: Rollback is fast, but database migrations must remain compatible during transition.
followups: Blue-green vs canary?
interview: Run old and new environments and switch traffic after validation.

title: Canary deployment
short: Send a small percentage of traffic to the new version before wider rollout.
answer: Use health and business metrics as rollout gates.
followups: What metrics gate rollout?
interview: Send a small percentage of traffic to the new version before wider rollout.

title: Distributed lock
short: A distributed lock coordinates exclusive ownership across instances.
answer: Leases/expiration and failure semantics are essential. Idempotency may be safer than locking.
followups: What if holder crashes?
interview: A distributed lock coordinates exclusive ownership across instances.

title: Strangler pattern
short: Incrementally replace slices of a legacy system.
answer: Route capabilities to new components, validate, then retire legacy paths.
followups: When is it better than rewrite?
interview: Incrementally replace slices of a legacy system.

answer: A resilience pattern that monitors calls to a downstream dependency; after a configured failure threshold is exceeded, it "opens" and fails fast (without even attempting the call) for a cooldown period, preventing a struggling downstream service from being overwhelmed further and protecting the caller's own threads/resources from piling up on slow failures. title: What is service discovery?
short: Service discovery lets services find healthy instances without hard-coding changing network locations.
answer: A registry or platform such as Kubernetes DNS can provide service locations. Discovery may be client-side or server-side. Health and lifecycle integration are essential so callers do not route to dead instances.
code:
order-service -> discovery -> order-service instance A
                              -> instance B
followups: Client-side vs server-side discovery?
How does Kubernetes provide discovery?
mistakes: Treating discovery as a replacement for health checks.
Hard-coding instance IP addresses.
interview: Service discovery decouples callers from instance locations. In container platforms, DNS/service abstractions often provide discovery without a separate registry.

title: Why are timeouts essential in microservices?
short: Without bounded timeouts, a slow dependency can hold resources until thread pools, connections and queues are exhausted.
answer: Every remote call should have a timeout appropriate to the business operation. Timeouts should be combined with bounded retries, circuit breaking and observability.
followups: How do you choose timeout values?
What happens if retries exceed the caller timeout?
mistakes: Relying on library defaults.
Setting a huge timeout to avoid transient failures.
interview: A timeout converts an unbounded wait into a controlled failure. I choose it from an end-to-end latency budget and downstream behavior.

title: How should retries be implemented?
short: Retries should be bounded, use backoff and jitter, and only target operations that are safe to repeat.
answer: Retrying every failure can amplify an outage. I retry transient network or service-unavailable failures with exponential backoff and jitter, cap attempts, and avoid retrying non-idempotent operations unless an idempotency mechanism exists.
followups: Why add jitter?
Retry vs circuit breaker?
How do you avoid duplicate writes?
mistakes: Infinite retries.
Retrying validation or authorization failures.
interview: Retries are a resilience tool, not a default for every exception. I use bounded attempts, backoff, jitter and idempotency where writes are involved.

title: Explain the Bulkhead pattern.
short: Bulkheads isolate resource pools so one failing dependency cannot consume all shared capacity.
answer: Separate thread pools, connection pools or concurrency limits can isolate workloads. If the payment dependency is slow, its capacity limit prevents it from exhausting resources needed by unrelated operations.
followups: Bulkhead vs circuit breaker?
What metric tells you a bulkhead is saturated?
mistakes: Thinking bulkhead retries failed calls.
Creating many pools without capacity planning.
interview: Bulkheads limit blast radius by isolating capacity. They complement timeouts and circuit breakers.

title: What is idempotency in an API?
short: An operation is idempotent when repeating the same logical request produces the same intended outcome.
answer: For payment or order creation, a client can send an idempotency key. The server stores the key and result so a retry does not create a second business operation.
followups: Where should idempotency keys be stored?
What if two requests with the same key arrive concurrently?
mistakes: Equating HTTP POST with automatically non-idempotent business behavior.
Using a non-unique key across unrelated operations.
interview: Idempotency protects business operations from duplicate delivery or client retries. I enforce uniqueness at the appropriate scope and define what happens for concurrent reuse.

title: Explain the Outbox pattern.
short: The service writes business state and an event record in the same local transaction, then publishes the outbox event asynchronously.
answer: The transaction commits the order row and outbox row together. A publisher reads unsent outbox rows and sends them to Kafka or another broker. Consumers must still be idempotent because publishing can be retried.
followups: How do you avoid publishing the same event twice?
Polling publisher vs CDC?
mistakes: Saying the outbox guarantees exactly-once end to end.
Deleting the outbox row before successful publication.
interview: Outbox closes the database-to-message consistency gap by committing the state change and event intent atomically. Delivery still needs idempotency.

title: Saga choreography vs orchestration?
short: Both coordinate distributed business transactions without a global database transaction; choreography uses events while orchestration uses a coordinator.
answer: In choreography, services react to events and emit the next event. In orchestration, a saga coordinator explicitly commands participants and handles compensations. Choreography can become hard to understand at high workflow complexity; orchestration adds a central workflow component.
followups: When would you choose orchestration?
What are compensating transactions?
mistakes: Calling compensation a database rollback.
Using choreography for a workflow with dozens of tightly coupled steps.
interview: A saga provides business-level coordination with local transactions and compensating actions. I choose choreography for simple flows and orchestration when workflow visibility and control matter.

title: What is eventual consistency?
short: Eventual consistency means replicas or services may temporarily disagree but converge if updates are successfully propagated.
answer: After an order is created, a read model or inventory service may lag for a short period. The design must define acceptable staleness and user behavior during that window.
code:
Order Service -> event -> Inventory
                 
                 read model catches up asynchronously
followups: How do you handle stale reads?
Strong vs eventual consistency trade-offs?
mistakes: Saying eventual consistency means data can be permanently wrong.
Using it without defining acceptable delay.
interview: Eventual consistency trades immediate global agreement for availability and decoupling. The system needs explicit rules for stale data and reconciliation.

title: What is distributed tracing?
short: Distributed tracing follows a request across services using propagated trace and span context.
answer: A trace represents the end-to-end request and spans represent work done by individual services or dependencies. Trace IDs let engineers correlate latency and failures across service boundaries.
code:
HTTP request
  traceId=abc
  Order span
    Payment span
    Inventory span
followups: Trace vs span?
How is context propagated?
mistakes: Treating logs as a complete substitute for tracing.
Creating a new trace at every service instead of propagating context.
interview: Tracing shows the path and latency breakdown of a distributed request. It is especially valuable when one user operation crosses multiple services.

title: What is CQRS?
short: CQRS separates command/write models from query/read models when their requirements differ significantly.
answer: The write side handles business invariants and commands, while the read side can be optimized for query patterns. CQRS does not automatically mean event sourcing or separate physical databases.
code:
POST /orders -> command model
GET /orders?customer=42 -> read model
followups: CQRS vs event sourcing?
When is CQRS unnecessary?
mistakes: Assuming CQRS is mandatory for microservices.
Equating CQRS with two databases in every implementation.
interview: CQRS is useful when read and write workloads or models have materially different needs. I avoid it when a simple CRUD model meets the requirements.

title: How do you prevent cascading failures?
short: Use timeouts, bounded retries, circuit breakers, bulkheads, load shedding and sensible dependency limits.
answer: A downstream outage can otherwise cause request queues to grow and exhaust threads. Resilience patterns should work together and be observable.
code:
Caller -> timeout -> circuit breaker -> fallback
                    -> bulkhead limits concurrency
followups: What is load shedding?
Why can retries make an outage worse?
mistakes: Adding retries without limits.
Using a fallback that performs another failing downstream call.
interview: I prevent cascades by bounding waiting and concurrency, failing fast where appropriate, and isolating dependencies. Then I monitor saturation and failure rates.

title: How would you handle duplicate Kafka messages?
short: Consumers should assume at-least-once delivery and make processing idempotent.
answer: A consumer can store a unique event ID or use a business key with a unique constraint. The state change and processed-event marker should be committed atomically where possible.
followups: Why can duplicates occur?
Does Kafka exactly-once remove all application duplicates?
mistakes: Assuming retries never duplicate messages.
Checking duplicates only in application memory.
interview: I design consumers for at-least-once delivery. Idempotency is enforced at a durable boundary, often with a unique key and transaction.

title: What is backpressure?
short: Backpressure prevents producers from overwhelming a consumer by controlling the rate or buffering of work.
answer: In streaming systems, a fast producer can create unbounded queues. Backpressure can use bounded queues, demand signals, rate limits or dropping strategies depending on business requirements.
followups: Backpressure vs rate limiting?
What should happen when the buffer is full?
mistakes: Assuming an unlimited queue solves throughput problems.
Ignoring memory growth.
interview: Backpressure makes overload behavior explicit. I choose bounded buffering, throttling or rejection based on whether data can be delayed or dropped.

title: What is service discovery in microservices?
short: Service discovery lets a service find another service dynamically instead of hard-coding host and port.
answer: A registry maintains service instances and their locations. A client-side or server-side discovery mechanism resolves a logical service name to a healthy instance. This becomes important when containers scale up, down or move.
code: Client -> service registry -> Order Service instances
followups: How does health checking work?
What is the difference between client-side and server-side discovery?
mistakes: Hard-coding pod IP addresses.
interview: Service discovery removes the need for callers to know physical instance locations. A registry or platform resolves the logical service name to an available instance.

title: Client-side vs server-side service discovery
short: Client-side discovery makes the caller choose an instance; server-side discovery delegates that choice to a load balancer or proxy.
answer: With client-side discovery, the client queries a registry and performs load balancing. With server-side discovery, the client calls a stable endpoint and the load balancer or platform resolves an instance.
code:
Client -> Registry -> choose instance
Client -> Load Balancer -> choose instance
followups: Which approach fits Kubernetes?
What are the trade-offs?
mistakes: Treating service discovery and load balancing as exactly the same component.
interview: Client-side discovery gives the application more control, while server-side discovery centralizes routing and keeps clients simpler.

title: What is a circuit breaker and why is it needed?
short: A circuit breaker stops repeatedly calling an unhealthy dependency so failures do not cascade.
answer: It normally moves through closed, open and half-open states. After repeated failures the circuit opens and fails fast; after a recovery delay it allows limited probes in half-open state.
code: Closed -> failures -> Open -> wait -> Half-open -> success -> Closed
followups: How do you configure failure thresholds?
Circuit breaker vs retry?
mistakes: Using a circuit breaker as a replacement for timeouts.
interview: A circuit breaker protects a system from repeatedly calling a failing dependency. It fails fast while the dependency is unhealthy and periodically probes for recovery.

title: Why should retries use exponential backoff and jitter?
short: Backoff spaces retry attempts and jitter prevents many clients from retrying simultaneously.
answer: Immediate retries can amplify load on a degraded service. Exponential backoff increases the delay after each failure, while jitter randomizes the delay so clients do not synchronize their retries.
followups: When should retries not be used?
How can retries cause a retry storm?
mistakes: Retrying non-idempotent operations blindly.
interview: I use bounded exponential backoff with jitter for transient failures and only retry operations that are safe to repeat.

title: What is the bulkhead pattern?
short: Bulkheads isolate resources so one failing workload cannot consume capacity needed by others.
answer: A service can maintain separate thread pools, connection pools or concurrency limits for independent dependencies. If one dependency becomes slow, its resource pool is exhausted without taking down unrelated traffic.
code:
Payments pool: 20 threads
Inventory pool: 20 threads
followups: How is bulkhead different from circuit breaker?
Where would you apply it?
mistakes: Using one shared unbounded executor for every downstream call.
interview: Bulkheads limit the blast radius of a dependency failure by isolating resources such as threads or connection pools.

title: How do retries, timeouts and circuit breakers work together?
short: They solve different failure modes and must be bounded so resilience mechanisms do not amplify failure.
answer: A typical call has a short timeout, a small number of retries with backoff, and a circuit breaker around the operation. The total retry budget must fit inside the caller SLA; otherwise retries can make latency worse.
code: Request SLA 3s -> timeout 800ms -> at most 2 retries -> circuit breaker
followups: What is retry amplification?
Where should the circuit breaker sit?
mistakes: Setting three retries with long timeouts that already exceed the SLA.
interview: Timeouts bound each attempt, retries handle transient failures, and the circuit breaker stops repeated calls when the dependency is persistently unhealthy.

title: What is idempotency in a REST API?
short: An operation is idempotent when repeating the same request produces the same intended business result.
answer: HTTP semantics alone are not enough for business idempotency. For operations such as payment creation, a client can send an idempotency key. The server stores the key and result and returns the same result for duplicate requests.
followups: How do you store idempotency keys?
What if two requests with the same key arrive concurrently?
mistakes: Generating a new payment every time the client retries.
interview: Idempotency prevents duplicate business effects when clients retry. A unique key plus durable storage and atomic handling makes the operation safe to repeat.

title: How would you design an idempotent payment API?
short: A payment API should atomically associate an idempotency key with the request and final business result.
answer: Persist a unique key scoped to the merchant or account, validate that a reused key has the same request fingerprint, process the payment within a transaction, and return the stored result for duplicates. For asynchronous providers, persist provider references and state transitions.
followups: How do you handle concurrent duplicate requests?
What if the provider times out after charging?
mistakes: Using an in-memory map as the only idempotency store.
interview: For payments I need durable idempotency keys, atomic uniqueness, request validation and explicit handling of unknown provider outcomes.

title: What is the Saga pattern?
short: Saga coordinates a business transaction across services using a sequence of local transactions and compensating actions.
answer: Each service commits locally and emits an event or calls the next step. If a later step fails, compensating actions undo the business effect of earlier steps. Saga can be choreography-based or orchestration-based.
code:
Order -> Reserve Inventory -> Charge Payment
Failure -> Release Inventory
followups: Saga vs two-phase commit?
How do you handle compensation failure?
mistakes: Calling compensation a database rollback.
interview: A Saga replaces one distributed transaction with multiple local transactions and explicit compensation when a later step cannot complete.

title: Saga choreography vs orchestration
short: Choreography uses events between services; orchestration uses a central coordinator that directs steps.
answer: Choreography reduces central coordination but can become difficult to understand as event dependencies grow. Orchestration makes workflow state explicit in one coordinator but introduces another component that must be reliable.
code:
Choreography: OrderCreated -> InventoryReserved -> PaymentRequested
Orchestration: SagaCoordinator -> each service
followups: When would you choose orchestration?
Can choreography create cyclic dependencies?
mistakes: Saying choreography has no coordination; the events themselves coordinate the workflow.
interview: I prefer choreography for small, loosely coupled workflows and orchestration when the transaction has many steps, branching or compensation rules.

title: What is the transactional outbox pattern?
short: The outbox pattern atomically stores a business change and the event to publish in the same local database transaction.
answer: Instead of updating a table and publishing directly to Kafka in separate operations, the service writes the business row and an outbox row in one transaction. A relay later publishes the outbox event. Consumers must still be idempotent because publishing can be retried.
code:
BEGIN
UPDATE orders ...
INSERT INTO outbox ...
COMMIT
followups: How does CDC fit the outbox pattern?
What happens if publishing fails?
mistakes: Assuming the database transaction can atomically commit with Kafka.
interview: Outbox closes the dual-write gap between the service database and a message broker by persisting the event alongside the business transaction.

title: What is change data capture (CDC)?
short: CDC captures database changes and makes them available to downstream consumers.
answer: A CDC connector reads database transaction changes, often from a database log, and publishes structured change events. It can feed search indexes, caches, analytics or an outbox relay without adding synchronous work to the request path.
code: DB transaction log -> CDC connector -> Kafka -> consumers
followups: CDC vs polling?
What are ordering considerations?
mistakes: Treating CDC as a replacement for business events in every use case.
interview: CDC observes database changes and can propagate them reliably, but business events may still be preferable when consumers need domain intent rather than row-level changes.

title: How do you prevent duplicate message processing?
short: Consumers should make processing idempotent because at-least-once delivery can produce duplicates.
answer: Store a unique event ID or business key with the processing result, or make the state transition naturally idempotent. The deduplication record and business update should be committed atomically when possible.
followups: What if the consumer crashes after the DB commit?
Exactly-once vs idempotent processing?
mistakes: Assuming a broker will never redeliver a message.
interview: I design consumers for at-least-once delivery and make the business effect idempotent, usually with a durable event ID or unique business constraint.

title: How do you preserve message ordering in Kafka?
short: Ordering is guaranteed only within a Kafka partition, so related events should use a stable partition key.
answer: If all events for an order use orderId as the key, Kafka routes them to the same partition and preserves their order there. Ordering across partitions is not guaranteed.
followups: What happens if partitions increase?
Can multiple consumers process one partition concurrently?
mistakes: Expecting global ordering across a topic with many partitions.
interview: Kafka guarantees order within a partition. I choose a business key such as orderId so related events stay ordered while unrelated keys can scale across partitions.

title: What is a Kafka consumer group?
short: A consumer group is a set of consumers that jointly process a topic, with each partition assigned to at most one consumer in the group at a time.
answer: Consumer groups provide horizontal consumption. If a topic has eight partitions, at most eight consumers in one group can actively consume partitions concurrently. Different groups receive their own copy of the stream.
followups: What triggers a rebalance?
Can two groups read the same message?
mistakes: Saying one partition is processed simultaneously by every consumer in the same group.
interview: A consumer group lets multiple instances share partitions for parallel processing, while separate groups independently consume the same topic.

title: What is Kafka consumer lag?
short: Consumer lag measures how far a consumer group is behind the latest available records.
answer: Lag can indicate slow processing, insufficient consumers, downstream bottlenecks or broker issues. I monitor lag together with processing latency and throughput instead of treating lag alone as the root cause.
followups: How do you reduce lag safely?
Can adding consumers always help?
mistakes: Adding consumers when the topic has fewer partitions.
interview: Lag is the gap between produced and consumed progress. I first identify whether the bottleneck is consumer CPU, downstream I/O, partitions or broker health before scaling.

title: What happens during a Kafka consumer rebalance?
short: A rebalance redistributes partitions among consumers in a group after membership or subscription changes.
answer: A consumer joining, leaving or failing can trigger reassignment. During the rebalance, ownership changes and processing can pause depending on the protocol and client configuration. Commit strategy matters because records may be replayed.
code:
Consumer A: P0,P1
Consumer B: P2,P3
Join C -> reassignment
followups: How can you reduce rebalance impact?
What is cooperative rebalancing?
mistakes: Assuming rebalancing means data loss.
interview: A rebalance changes partition ownership. Good consumer configuration, graceful shutdown and appropriate commit behavior reduce pauses and duplicate work.

title: At-most-once vs at-least-once vs exactly-once delivery
short: These describe whether messages can be lost, duplicated or processed with stronger atomicity guarantees.
answer: At-most-once may lose messages but avoids redelivery. At-least-once can duplicate messages and is common for reliable processing. Exactly-once requires carefully scoped transactional semantics and still needs business-level reasoning across external systems.
code:
At-most-once: commit -> process
At-least-once: process -> commit
followups: Why is exactly-once difficult end to end?
How do you design for at-least-once?
mistakes: Calling Kafka exactly-once equivalent to exactly-once business effects across databases and APIs.
interview: I usually design business consumers for at-least-once delivery with idempotent effects. Exactly-once can be achieved in bounded systems but is not a magic end-to-end property.

title: How do you handle poison messages in Kafka?
short: A poison message repeatedly fails processing and can block progress if it is not isolated.
answer: Use bounded retries, then route the failed record to a dead-letter topic or quarantine mechanism with enough metadata for investigation. The consumer should commit or otherwise advance according to a deliberate failure policy so one bad record does not cause an infinite retry loop.
followups: Should DLT messages be retried automatically?
What metadata should be stored?
mistakes: Infinite immediate retries on the main topic.
interview: I use bounded retries and a dead-letter path for poison messages, preserving the original payload, error, attempt count and correlation information.

title: What is a dead-letter queue or topic?
short: A dead-letter destination stores messages that cannot be processed successfully after the configured retry policy.
answer: It isolates bad messages from the normal flow while preserving them for investigation or controlled replay. The DLQ should have monitoring, retention and an operational replay strategy.
followups: How do you replay a DLQ safely?
Should every exception go to DLQ?
mistakes: Treating DLQ as permanent data deletion.
interview: A DLQ is a controlled quarantine for failed messages. It should be observable and replayable after the underlying problem is fixed.

title: What is backpressure in event-driven systems?
short: Backpressure prevents producers or upstream work from overwhelming a slower consumer.
answer: Controls include bounded queues, consumer concurrency limits, rate limiting, broker retention, flow control and load shedding. The right choice depends on whether data may be delayed, dropped or must be durably buffered.
code:
Producer rate: 10k/s
Consumer capacity: 5k/s
Need buffering or throttling
followups: How does Kafka help absorb bursts?
What if the backlog never drains?
mistakes: Using unbounded in-memory queues.
interview: Backpressure keeps a fast producer from exhausting downstream resources. I use bounded buffering and explicit policies for delay, throttling or load shedding.

title: How would you design an order event flow for reliability?
short: A reliable order flow uses durable state, transactional event publication, idempotent consumers and observable retry paths.
answer: Create the order and outbox event atomically. Publish to Kafka, partition by orderId, consume with idempotent inventory/payment handlers, use bounded retries and DLT, and expose correlation IDs and lag metrics.
followups: How do you recover from duplicate events?
What if Kafka is temporarily unavailable?
mistakes: Publishing directly after the DB commit without an outbox.
interview: I would use an outbox for atomic local persistence, Kafka keyed by orderId for ordering, idempotent consumers and explicit retry/DLT handling.

title: What are correlation IDs and why are they useful?
short: A correlation ID is a stable request identifier propagated across logs and downstream calls.
answer: When a request crosses several services, the same correlation or trace identifier lets operators search related logs quickly. It should not be treated as an authentication credential or sensitive data container.
followups: Correlation ID vs trace ID?
Where should it be generated?
mistakes: Generating a new ID at every service without preserving the incoming context.
interview: Correlation IDs provide a simple way to connect logs across services. In modern tracing systems, trace IDs can serve a similar purpose with richer context.

title: What are the four golden signals?
short: The four golden signals are latency, traffic, errors and saturation.
answer: They provide a compact view of service health: request latency, request volume, error rate and how close resources are to capacity. They complement application-specific business metrics.
followups: What business metrics would you add?
How do you alert on latency?
mistakes: Monitoring CPU alone as service health.
interview: The golden signals are latency, traffic, errors and saturation. They help detect user-visible degradation and resource pressure.

title: Liveness vs readiness probes in Kubernetes
short: Liveness asks whether a container should be restarted; readiness asks whether it should receive traffic.
answer: A readiness failure should remove the instance from service without necessarily restarting it. Liveness should detect an unrecoverable process state and be conservative to avoid restart loops.
followups: Why should liveness not depend on a database?
What happens when readiness fails?
mistakes: Using a slow dependency check for liveness.
interview: Readiness controls traffic eligibility, while liveness controls restart decisions. I keep liveness lightweight so a temporary dependency outage does not cause restart storms.

title: What is graceful shutdown in a microservice?
short: Graceful shutdown stops new work, lets in-flight work finish within a deadline and closes resources cleanly.
answer: On termination, the instance should be removed from service discovery/load balancing, stop accepting new requests, finish or cancel active work, commit/rollback transactions and close consumers or connections.
followups: Why is readiness important during shutdown?
How do you handle long-running requests?
mistakes: Immediately killing the process on deployment.
interview: Graceful shutdown prevents dropped in-flight requests and partial work by draining traffic before the process exits.

title: How do you achieve zero-downtime deployments?
short: Zero-downtime deployment keeps enough healthy capacity available while replacing old instances.
answer: Use rolling or blue-green deployment, readiness checks, backward-compatible API/database changes, connection draining and fast rollback. Database migrations should follow an expand-and-contract strategy when schemas must coexist across versions.
code: v1 + v2 -> migrate -> switch -> remove v1
followups: What is expand-and-contract?
How do you roll back a database change?
mistakes: Deploying a breaking schema and application change simultaneously.
interview: I combine rolling or blue-green deployment with readiness, graceful shutdown and backward-compatible schema changes so old and new versions can coexist during rollout.

title: How do you make database schema changes safe across microservice deployments?
short: Schema changes should be backward compatible while multiple application versions may run during deployment.
answer: Use expand-and-contract: add nullable/new structures first, deploy code that can read both forms, backfill data, switch writes, then remove the old structure after all old instances are gone.
code: 1 add column -> 2 dual read/write -> 3 backfill -> 4 switch -> 5 remove
followups: How do you handle renaming a column?
Why can a direct DROP break rolling deployments?
mistakes: Assuming deployment is instantaneous.
interview: During rolling deployments, old and new application versions can coexist, so database changes must be compatible with both.

title: What is a service mesh?
short: A service mesh provides infrastructure-level communication features between services, often through sidecars or ambient proxies.
answer: It can provide mTLS, traffic routing, retries, telemetry and policy without putting every networking concern into application code. It also adds operational complexity and another layer to debug.
code: Service A -> proxy -> proxy -> Service B
followups: Service mesh vs API Gateway?
When would you avoid a service mesh?
mistakes: Assuming a mesh removes all application-level resilience decisions.
interview: A service mesh handles common service-to-service networking concerns consistently, but it does not replace domain logic or all application resilience design.

title: How do you avoid a single point of failure in an API Gateway?
short: Run multiple gateway instances behind a highly available load balancer and keep gateway state external or stateless where possible.
answer: Gateway instances should be horizontally scalable. Authentication metadata, rate-limit state or sessions that must be shared should use a resilient external store or distributed mechanism.
followups: What if the gateway itself is overloaded?
How do you deploy gateway configuration safely?
mistakes: Running one gateway instance because it is stateless.
interview: I remove gateway single points of failure through multiple instances, health checks, horizontal scaling and externalized shared state.

title: How do you prevent cascading failures in microservices?
short: Cascading failures occur when one slow or failing dependency consumes resources across callers until the whole system degrades.
answer: Use timeouts, bounded retries, circuit breakers, bulkheads, concurrency limits, load shedding, caching where appropriate and graceful degradation. Monitor dependency latency and saturation so protection activates before the caller is exhausted.
code: A slow B -> A threads blocked -> A fails -> upstream retries A
followups: Why can retries worsen cascading failures?
What is load shedding?
mistakes: Adding retries everywhere without budgets.
interview: Cascading failures are controlled by limiting dependency impact: short timeouts, bounded retries, isolation, circuit breaking and graceful degradation.

title: How do you handle partial failure in a distributed workflow?
short: Partial failure means some steps succeed while others fail or become unknown.
answer: Persist workflow state, use idempotent commands, explicit statuses and compensating actions where appropriate. For external systems, design for unknown outcomes and reconciliation rather than assuming timeout means failure.
followups: What is reconciliation?
How do you handle an unknown payment result?
mistakes: Treating a timeout as proof that the operation did not happen.
interview: In distributed workflows, a timeout can mean unknown outcome. I persist state, use idempotency and reconciliation to converge the workflow safely.

title: What is the difference between synchronous and asynchronous communication?
short: Synchronous communication waits for an immediate response; asynchronous communication decouples sender and receiver in time.
answer: REST/gRPC is commonly synchronous and useful when the caller needs an immediate result. Messaging is useful for long-running, bursty or independently scalable workflows, but introduces eventual consistency and operational complexity.
code:
Sync: A -> B -> response
Async: A -> broker -> B
followups: When would you prefer async?
How do you expose async status to clients?
mistakes: Using async messaging for every CRUD call.
interview: I choose synchronous calls when the caller needs an immediate answer and asynchronous messaging when decoupling, buffering or independent processing is more valuable.

title: REST vs gRPC for microservice communication
short: REST is broadly interoperable and HTTP-friendly; gRPC uses HTTP/2 and strongly typed protobuf contracts for efficient service-to-service communication.
answer: REST is convenient for public APIs and browser integrations. gRPC can provide compact payloads, streaming and generated clients for internal services. Choice depends on ecosystem, observability and operational requirements.
code:
REST: JSON over HTTP
gRPC: Protobuf over HTTP/2
followups: Can browsers call gRPC directly?
What about streaming?
mistakes: Choosing gRPC only because it is faster in benchmarks.
interview: REST is often the better public API boundary, while gRPC can be attractive for internal typed, high-throughput or streaming communication.

title: What is API versioning and how would you implement it?
short: API versioning lets a service evolve contracts while supporting existing clients during migration.
answer: Common approaches include URI, header or media-type versioning. I prefer backward-compatible additive changes where possible and use explicit versions when semantics or contracts must break.
followups: URI vs header versioning?
How do you deprecate v1?
mistakes: Creating a new version for every additive field.
interview: I avoid unnecessary versions by making additive changes backward compatible. When semantics break, I expose a new contract and give clients a migration window.

title: What is rate limiting in an API?
short: Rate limiting controls how many requests a client can make over a period or token budget.
answer: Algorithms include fixed window, sliding window, token bucket and leaky bucket. Distributed deployments need shared or coordinated state if limits must apply across instances.
followups: Token bucket vs leaky bucket?
Where should rate limiting happen?
mistakes: Using only an in-memory counter behind multiple instances.
interview: Rate limiting protects capacity and fairness. For distributed gateways, the limiting state must be coordinated or the limit becomes per-instance rather than global.

title: What is load shedding?
short: Load shedding deliberately rejects lower-priority work when a system is overloaded to preserve critical functionality.
answer: Examples include returning 429, rejecting optional requests, reducing expensive features or applying priority queues. The goal is graceful degradation rather than letting every request time out.
followups: How is load shedding different from rate limiting?
How do you choose what to shed?
mistakes: Letting queues grow without bound until the process crashes.
interview: Load shedding is an overload protection mechanism. It intentionally sacrifices some work so the core system remains responsive.

title: How would you design a multi-region microservice?
short: A multi-region design distributes service instances and data across geographic regions to reduce latency and improve availability.
answer: Key decisions include active-active vs active-passive, data replication, conflict handling, traffic routing, regional failure detection and recovery objectives. Not every service needs global active-active writes.
code: Users -> Global DNS -> Region A / Region B
followups: How do you handle cross-region writes?
RPO vs RTO?
mistakes: Assuming multi-region automatically means strongly consistent global data.
interview: Multi-region improves resilience and latency but introduces replication and failure-mode complexity. I choose a data strategy based on RPO, RTO and consistency requirements.

title: RPO vs RTO in disaster recovery
short: RPO is the maximum acceptable data loss measured in time; RTO is the maximum acceptable recovery time.
answer: For example, RPO of five minutes means losing up to five minutes of data may be acceptable. RTO of 30 minutes means the service should recover within 30 minutes. These targets drive backup and replication architecture.
followups: How do backups affect RPO?
How do you test RTO?
mistakes: Confusing RPO with downtime.
interview: RPO defines tolerated data loss; RTO defines tolerated recovery time. Both should be explicit before selecting a disaster-recovery design.

title: How do you design a distributed lock?
short: A distributed lock coordinates access to a shared resource across multiple service instances.
answer: A robust design needs ownership, expiration/lease, safe release and behavior when the holder pauses or loses connectivity. For critical correctness, database constraints or transactional state transitions may be safer than a lock.
followups: Why can a distributed lock expire while work is still running?
How do you avoid deleting another owner's lock?
mistakes: Using a random delete without checking ownership.
interview: Distributed locks are difficult because process pauses and network partitions exist. I use leases and owner tokens, and prefer database invariants when they can express the business rule.

title: What is the CAP theorem?
short: CAP says that during a network partition, a distributed system cannot simultaneously guarantee both strong consistency and availability for all operations.
answer: The practical trade-off appears when nodes cannot communicate. A system must choose whether to reject or delay some operations to preserve consistency, or continue serving potentially divergent data for availability.
followups: Does CAP mean you can only choose two of C,A,P?
How does this relate to databases?
mistakes: Saying a system permanently chooses two letters regardless of conditions.
interview: CAP is specifically about behavior during partitions. P is a reality in distributed systems; the meaningful trade-off is consistency versus availability under that partition.

title: What is event sourcing?
short: Event sourcing stores the sequence of domain events as the source of truth rather than only the latest state.
answer: Current state can be rebuilt by replaying events, and snapshots can reduce replay cost. It provides a strong audit history but complicates schema evolution, querying and operational recovery.
followups: Event sourcing vs event-driven architecture?
How do you version events?
mistakes: Calling any Kafka-based system event sourced.
interview: Event sourcing makes events the durable source of truth. Event-driven architecture only means components communicate through events; it does not require event history as the system of record.

title: What is the strangler fig pattern?
short: The strangler pattern incrementally replaces a legacy system by routing selected capabilities to new services.
answer: A facade or gateway directs some functionality to the new implementation while the old system continues serving the rest. Over time, more capabilities move until the legacy component can be retired.
followups: How do you keep data consistent during migration?
What makes strangler safer than a big-bang rewrite?
mistakes: Trying to migrate all functionality at once.
interview: The strangler pattern reduces migration risk by moving bounded capabilities incrementally while the legacy system continues operating.

title: How would you migrate a monolith to microservices safely?
short: A safe migration starts with business boundaries and incremental extraction rather than splitting classes mechanically.
answer: Identify bounded contexts, isolate a capability, define an API/event contract, establish observability, move data ownership carefully, route traffic gradually and retire the old path only after proving correctness.
followups: How do you choose the first service?
What is the data migration strategy?
mistakes: Creating dozens of services from technical layers.
interview: I extract cohesive business capabilities incrementally, keep contracts explicit, migrate ownership carefully and use observability plus gradual traffic shifting to reduce risk.

title: What is a bounded context?
short: A bounded context defines a boundary within which a domain model and terminology have a consistent meaning.
answer: The same word can mean different things in different contexts. Bounded contexts help services own cohesive models instead of sharing one giant domain model across the system.
code:
Order context: Customer
Billing context: Account
followups: Bounded context vs microservice?
Can one context contain multiple services?
mistakes: Treating bounded context as exactly one deployable service.
interview: A bounded context is a domain boundary, not a deployment rule. A microservice can implement a context, but the concepts are not identical.

title: What is the dual-write problem?
short: Dual write occurs when one business operation updates two independent systems without a shared atomic transaction.
answer: For example, writing an order to a database and then publishing Kafka can leave one side updated and the other missing if the process fails between operations. Outbox, CDC or reconciliation patterns address the gap.
code: DB write ✓ -> process crashes -> Kafka publish ✗
followups: Why not simply publish before the DB write?
Outbox vs two-phase commit?
mistakes: Assuming two sequential operations are atomic.
interview: Two independent writes cannot be assumed atomic. I use an outbox or another consistency pattern when the database change and event publication must stay aligned.

title: How do you handle an external API timeout when the operation may have succeeded?
short: A timeout creates an unknown outcome: the remote service may have completed the operation even though the response was lost.
answer: Use an idempotency key when supported, query the provider by reference when possible, persist a pending/unknown state and reconcile asynchronously. Never blindly retry a non-idempotent operation.
code: POST payment(idempotencyKey) -> timeout -> GET status -> reconcile
followups: What if the provider has no status API?
How do you communicate status to the user?
mistakes: Immediately issuing a second charge.
interview: A timeout is not proof of failure. I preserve an unknown state, use idempotency or reconciliation and only finalize the business state when the outcome is known.

title: What is a fallback in resilience design?
short: A fallback is a deliberate degraded response used when a dependency cannot be called successfully.
answer: Examples include cached data, default recommendations or an asynchronous acceptance response. A fallback must be semantically safe; returning fake critical data can be worse than failing.
followups: When should you not use a fallback?
Fallback vs retry?
mistakes: Returning stale payment status as if it were current.
interview: A fallback provides controlled degradation when a dependency fails. I only use one when the degraded result is safe and understandable to the caller.

title: What is a timeout budget or latency budget?
short: A latency budget is the maximum time a request can spend across all downstream operations while meeting its SLA.
answer: If an endpoint has a 1-second SLA, individual calls cannot each be allowed to consume one second. The service must allocate a budget across parallel and sequential dependencies and reserve time for its own work.
code: SLA 1000ms -> downstream A 300ms + B 300ms + local 200ms + margin
followups: Why should retries share the same budget?
How do parallel calls change budgeting?
mistakes: Giving every downstream call an independent full SLA timeout.
interview: Timeouts should fit within the overall latency budget. Otherwise a service can meet each local timeout while violating the user-facing SLA.

title: What is connection pooling in microservices?
short: Connection pooling reuses established network or database connections instead of creating one for every request.
answer: Pools reduce handshake overhead and control concurrency. The pool size must match downstream capacity; too many connections can overload a database or remote service.
followups: How do you choose pool size?
What happens when the pool is exhausted?
mistakes: Increasing the pool indefinitely to fix latency.
interview: Connection pools improve reuse and provide a concurrency limit. I size them based on workload and downstream capacity, then monitor pool exhaustion.

title: How would you troubleshoot a slow microservice endpoint?
short: Start with user-visible latency, then trace the request across application, network and data dependencies.
answer: Check metrics for latency/errors/saturation, inspect traces for slow spans, examine logs with correlation IDs, verify thread and connection pools, inspect database query plans and downstream latency. Reproduce under controlled load before changing limits.
code: Request -> trace -> slow span -> DB query -> EXPLAIN
followups: How do you distinguish CPU from I/O bottlenecks?
What metrics would you inspect first?
mistakes: Increasing timeouts without finding the bottleneck.
interview: I start with metrics and traces, identify the slowest dependency or resource, validate with logs and profiling/query plans, then make a targeted change.

title: How do you handle a downstream service that becomes slow but not completely unavailable?
short: A slow dependency can be more dangerous than a hard failure because it holds resources for longer.
answer: Use aggressive timeouts, concurrency limits/bulkheads, circuit breaking based on slow-call thresholds, bounded retries only where safe, and fallbacks. Protect the caller before its threads or connections are exhausted.
followups: Why can slow calls open a circuit breaker?
How does queueing affect latency?
mistakes: Waiting indefinitely because the dependency is technically up.
interview: I treat sustained slowness as a failure mode. Timeouts and isolation prevent slow downstream work from consuming all caller capacity.

title: What is health-check endpoint design in microservices?
short: Health endpoints should distinguish process health from dependency readiness and should be cheap enough for frequent probing.
answer: A liveness endpoint can answer whether the process is functioning. Readiness can include critical dependency checks, but those checks should have bounded timeouts and not create a dependency storm.
followups: What should liveness check?
Should readiness check every dependency?
mistakes: Making health checks execute expensive business queries.
interview: Health checks should be lightweight and purposeful: liveness for process health, readiness for whether the instance should receive traffic.

title: What is centralized configuration in microservices?
short: Centralized configuration keeps environment-specific settings outside application binaries and provides a consistent way to manage them.
answer: Services can load configuration from a configuration service, environment variables or a secret manager. Sensitive values should be stored in a secret system rather than ordinary configuration.
code:
Service -> Config Store
Service -> Secret Manager
followups: How do you refresh configuration safely?
Config service failure behavior?
mistakes: Storing passwords in Git.
interview: Centralized configuration separates deployment settings from code. Secrets require stronger controls, and services need a safe startup/failure strategy when configuration is unavailable.

title: Why should secrets not be stored in application.yml or Git?
short: Secrets committed to source control can leak through repositories, logs, artifacts or developer machines.
answer: Use a secret manager or protected runtime environment, inject secrets at runtime, rotate them and audit access. Configuration files can reference secret keys without containing secret values.
followups: How do you rotate a secret without downtime?
What about encrypted Git secrets?
mistakes: Hard-coding credentials in source code.
interview: Secrets should be externalized and rotated. Encryption at rest is not enough if access control, logging or rotation are weak.

title: What is horizontal vs vertical scaling in microservices?
short: Horizontal scaling adds more instances; vertical scaling gives an instance more resources.
answer: Stateless services are usually easy to scale horizontally. Vertical scaling can be simpler for some workloads but has hardware limits and creates larger failure units.
code:
Horizontal: 3 pods -> 10 pods
Vertical: 2 CPU -> 8 CPU
followups: What makes a service horizontally scalable?
How does a database scale differently?
mistakes: Assuming adding application instances fixes a database bottleneck.
interview: Horizontal scaling increases instance count and resilience, while vertical scaling increases per-instance capacity. The bottleneck must be identified before choosing either.

title: How do you make a microservice stateless?
short: A stateless service does not depend on local process memory for durable client session or workflow state.
answer: Store durable state in databases, caches or external workflow stores. Local memory can still be used as a cache if losing it does not break correctness. Statelessness makes replacement and horizontal scaling easier.
followups: Can you use local caching in a stateless service?
Where should sessions live?
mistakes: Keeping checkout state only in one pod's memory.
interview: Stateless means the service instance is replaceable without losing required state. Durable state belongs in shared infrastructure.

title: What is distributed rate limiting?
short: Distributed rate limiting coordinates request limits across multiple application instances.
answer: A shared store such as Redis can maintain counters or token buckets, or an API gateway/service mesh can enforce limits. The design must account for clocking, atomic updates and store availability.
followups: What if Redis is unavailable?
How do token buckets work atomically?
mistakes: Using local counters when a global limit is required.
interview: For a global limit, instances need coordinated state or a centralized enforcement point. The failure policy must also be explicit.

title: How do you design an API for long-running asynchronous jobs?
short: The API accepts work, returns a job identifier and lets the client query status or receive completion notification.
answer: POST /reports can return 202 Accepted with a job ID. A worker processes the job and persists status such as QUEUED, RUNNING, SUCCEEDED or FAILED. The status API should be idempotent and observable.
followups: Why use 202?
How do you handle duplicate submissions?
mistakes: Keeping the HTTP connection open for minutes.
interview: For long-running work I return an asynchronous job ID, persist state, process via workers and expose a status or callback mechanism.

title: What is graceful degradation?
short: Graceful degradation keeps core functionality available while reducing optional functionality under failure or load.
answer: Examples include serving cached data, disabling recommendations or reducing page detail while preserving checkout. Degraded behavior should be explicit and tested.
followups: How do you decide what is optional?
How do you test degraded modes?
mistakes: Returning successful responses with invalid critical data.
interview: Graceful degradation protects critical user journeys by intentionally reducing nonessential functionality rather than letting the entire request fail.

title: How do you design a reliable notification microservice?
short: A reliable notification service separates request acceptance, scheduling, delivery and provider-specific retries.
answer: Persist notification intent, publish work to a queue, use provider adapters, idempotency keys and bounded retries, route permanent failures to a DLQ, and expose delivery status. Email/SMS providers can return unknown outcomes, so provider references are important.
followups: How do you prevent duplicate SMS?
How do you retry provider failures?
mistakes: Sending directly in the API request without durable work state.
interview: I would persist the notification intent, process asynchronously, use idempotent delivery keys, bounded retries and a DLQ, and track provider outcomes.

title: How do you design an order service for high traffic?
short: A high-traffic order service should isolate writes, protect dependencies and scale stateless application nodes horizontally.
answer: Use stateless APIs, database indexing and partitioning where needed, asynchronous events for downstream work, idempotent order creation, caching for read-heavy data and strong observability. Keep payment and inventory ownership in their own services.
code:
Client -> LB -> Order API -> DB
                  -> Outbox -> Kafka
followups: Where would you use caching?
How do you avoid duplicate orders?
mistakes: Sharing one database schema and transaction across every service.
interview: I keep order ownership local, make the API idempotent, scale stateless instances, use an outbox for events and isolate downstream failures.

title: What is a distributed transaction and why is it hard?
short: A distributed transaction spans multiple resource managers or services and requires coordination across failure-prone network boundaries.
answer: A local database transaction can atomically update its own data, but another service may commit independently. Network failures create partial success. Two-phase commit can coordinate some resources but adds blocking and operational complexity.
code: Service A commit ✓ -> network failure -> Service B unknown
followups: Saga alternative?
Why not use one global transaction?
mistakes: Assuming @Transactional crosses service boundaries.
interview: A Spring transaction is normally local to a resource manager. Cross-service transactions require distributed coordination or business-level patterns such as Saga and compensation.

title: What is the role of an anti-corruption layer?
short: An anti-corruption layer prevents a legacy or external model from leaking into a new domain model.
answer: The layer translates requests, responses and concepts between bounded contexts. It reduces coupling and lets the new service evolve independently of the legacy representation.
code: Legacy DTO -> ACL -> New Domain Model
followups: When is an ACL useful?
Can an API gateway be an ACL?
mistakes: Passing legacy entities directly into new business logic.
interview: An anti-corruption layer translates models at a boundary so a new domain is not forced to adopt an external or legacy model.

title: What is contract testing in microservices?
short: Contract testing verifies that a service provider and consumer agree on the API contract.
answer: Consumer-driven contracts can specify expected requests and responses. The provider verifies those expectations during CI, reducing integration surprises without requiring every consumer to run in a full environment.
followups: Contract test vs end-to-end test?
How do you version contracts?
mistakes: Testing only that a controller starts successfully.
interview: Contract tests verify compatibility between service boundaries and catch breaking changes earlier than full end-to-end tests.

title: What is consumer-driven contract testing?
short: Consumer-driven contracts let consumers define the interactions they rely on, which the provider verifies.
answer: A consumer publishes expectations for an endpoint or message. The provider runs those contracts in CI. This focuses provider compatibility on actual consumer needs.
followups: What if multiple consumers have conflicting expectations?
How do contracts work with Kafka?
mistakes: Treating a contract as an implementation detail instead of an API compatibility promise.
interview: Consumer-driven contracts make provider compatibility explicit and testable against real consumer expectations.

title: How should microservices handle backward-compatible API changes?
short: Prefer additive changes that old clients can ignore.
answer: Add optional fields, avoid changing existing meanings, support old enum values, and introduce new endpoints or versions only when semantics must change. Deprecate gradually with telemetry to identify remaining consumers.
followups: Why are enum changes risky?
How do you know when it is safe to remove old behavior?
mistakes: Renaming a field without supporting the old field.
interview: I prefer additive, backward-compatible changes and use consumer telemetry to decide when deprecated contracts can be removed.

title: What is a retry storm?
short: A retry storm occurs when many clients retry failed or slow requests simultaneously, increasing load on an already degraded dependency.
answer: Retries should be bounded, use exponential backoff and jitter, and respect an overall deadline. Circuit breakers and load shedding can stop repeated calls when failure persists.
followups: How does jitter help?
What is retry amplification?
mistakes: Immediate fixed-interval retries from every client.
interview: A retry storm amplifies load during failure. Backoff, jitter, deadlines and circuit breaking prevent resilience logic from becoming the outage multiplier.

title: How do you handle clock skew between microservices?
short: Clock skew means different machines may disagree about the current time.
answer: Use synchronized clocks such as NTP, avoid using wall-clock time for strict ordering, and prefer monotonic clocks for measuring durations. Distributed systems should tolerate small timestamp differences.
code:
Duration -> monotonic clock
Event time -> UTC timestamp
followups: Why are monotonic clocks important?
Can timestamps establish total event order?
mistakes: Assuming two timestamps from different machines are perfectly comparable.
interview: Wall clocks are useful for timestamps but not strict duration or global ordering. I use monotonic clocks for elapsed time and explicit sequence/versioning when order matters.

title: How do you design distributed id generation?
short: Distributed IDs need to be unique across instances without requiring one central bottleneck.
answer: Options include UUIDs, database sequences, Snowflake-style IDs or application-generated sortable IDs. The choice depends on ordering, size, index locality and coordination requirements.
code:
UUID -> globally unique
Snowflake -> timestamp + node + sequence
followups: UUID vs database sequence?
Why can random UUIDs affect database indexes?
mistakes: Using timestamps alone as unique IDs.
interview: I choose an ID strategy based on uniqueness, ordering and database indexing needs. UUIDs remove coordination; Snowflake-style IDs add sortable structure.

title: What is database-per-service and why is it recommended?
short: Database-per-service means each service owns its persistent data and other services access it through APIs or events.
answer: It preserves service autonomy and prevents direct schema coupling. Cross-service queries are handled through APIs, read models, events or dedicated reporting stores.
code:
Order Service -> Order DB
Inventory Service -> Inventory DB
followups: Can services share the same physical database server?
How do you perform cross-service reporting?
mistakes: Joining another service's tables directly.
interview: The key is ownership and independent schema evolution. Physical infrastructure can be shared, but services should not directly depend on each other's tables.

title: How do you handle cross-service reporting when each service owns its data?
short: Build a reporting/read model from events or controlled data pipelines instead of querying service tables directly.
answer: Publish domain or CDC events into a reporting pipeline, transform them into an analytics store or read database, and accept the required freshness. This preserves ownership while supporting cross-domain queries.
followups: How fresh does the report need to be?
CDC vs domain events?
mistakes: Creating foreign keys across service-owned databases.
interview: Cross-service reporting should use an intentional read model or analytics pipeline. Direct table joins couple services and undermine independent ownership.

title: What is a distributed cache and what problems does it introduce?
short: A distributed cache stores reusable data across multiple service instances, but introduces consistency, invalidation and availability concerns.
answer: Redis is a common choice. Design TTLs, eviction, stampede protection and behavior when the cache is unavailable. Never make correctness depend solely on a cache unless the system explicitly supports that model.
followups: Cache-aside vs write-through?
How do you prevent cache stampede?
mistakes: Assuming cached data is always current.
interview: A distributed cache reduces latency and database load but introduces stale data and failure modes. I define invalidation, TTL and fallback behavior explicitly.

title: What is cache stampede and how do you prevent it?
short: A cache stampede occurs when many requests miss or expire the same key and simultaneously hit the backend.
answer: Use request coalescing/single-flight, randomized TTLs, stale-while-revalidate, warm-up or locking with careful timeouts. The goal is to limit concurrent backend refreshes.
followups: What is cache penetration?
Why add jitter to TTL?
mistakes: Using a global lock with no timeout.
interview: Cache stampede protection prevents a synchronized set of misses from overwhelming the source of truth.

title: What is cache-aside pattern?
short: In cache-aside, the application reads the cache first and loads from the database on a miss, then populates the cache.
answer: Writes normally update the database and invalidate or refresh the cache. It is simple but requires careful invalidation and tolerates temporary staleness.
followups: When is write-through better?
What happens if cache.put fails after DB commit?
mistakes: Treating the cache as the source of truth.
interview: Cache-aside keeps the database authoritative. The application controls cache loading and invalidation and must tolerate cache failures.

title: What is eventual cache consistency?
short: A cache can temporarily contain a value different from the database or another replica.
answer: Asynchronous invalidation, TTLs or event propagation create a window where readers see stale data. The application should define whether that staleness is acceptable for each use case.
followups: How do you invalidate across instances?
When is stale data unacceptable?
mistakes: Using a cache for authorization decisions without a freshness strategy.
interview: Cache consistency is a business decision. I define the allowed staleness and choose invalidation or refresh mechanisms accordingly.

title: How do you design retries for Kafka consumers?
short: Consumer retries should avoid blocking healthy records indefinitely while preserving failed records for diagnosis.
answer: Use bounded in-process retries for transient errors, retry topics with backoff for longer delays, and a DLT for exhausted messages. Commit/acknowledgment behavior must match the chosen retry flow.
followups: Retry topic vs consumer sleep?
How do you preserve ordering?
mistakes: Sleeping a consumer thread for minutes on every failure.
interview: I separate transient retry from permanent failure, use backoff and a DLT, and choose the retry topology based on ordering and throughput requirements.

title: How do you handle schema evolution in Kafka events?
short: Event schemas should evolve compatibly so producers and consumers can be deployed independently.
answer: Use schema registries and compatibility rules where appropriate, prefer additive optional fields, and avoid changing the meaning or type of existing fields. Version events when semantics genuinely change.
code: Event v1 + optional field -> consumers upgrade gradually
followups: Backward vs forward compatibility?
What about Avro/Protobuf?
mistakes: Deleting a field while old consumers still require it.
interview: Schema evolution is a compatibility problem. I prefer additive changes, explicit compatibility rules and versioning when the event meaning changes.

title: What is a correlation between Kafka partition key and ordering?
short: The partition key determines which partition receives a record and therefore which ordering domain it belongs to.
answer: All events requiring order should share the same key. A poor key can create hot partitions, so ordering requirements must be balanced against distribution.
followups: How do hot partitions happen?
Can you change the key later?
mistakes: Using random keys when per-entity ordering is required.
interview: The key defines the ordering scope. I choose a stable business key and check its distribution so one high-volume key does not create a hot partition.

title: What is a hot partition in Kafka?
short: A hot partition receives disproportionately more records than others and becomes a throughput bottleneck.
answer: It can happen when the partition key has low cardinality or one entity generates much more traffic. Mitigation may involve better keys, sharding a hot entity or increasing partitions when semantics allow.
followups: How would you diagnose it?
What does increasing partitions change?
mistakes: Assuming adding consumers fixes a single hot partition.
interview: A hot partition is a skew problem. I inspect partition traffic, then change the key or workload distribution while preserving required ordering.

title: How do you design an event-driven system for replay?
short: Replayable event systems retain enough immutable event history and deterministic consumer logic to rebuild derived state.
answer: Keep durable events for an appropriate retention period, version schemas, make consumers idempotent, isolate replay consumer groups and ensure side effects are controlled so replay does not resend real-world actions accidentally.
code: events -> new consumer group -> rebuild read model
followups: How do you prevent replay from charging a payment twice?
Why are deterministic consumers important?
mistakes: Replaying production events directly into irreversible side effects.
interview: Replay is safest for rebuilding derived state. Irreversible side effects need deduplication, simulation or separate handling.

title: What is the difference between orchestration and choreography in microservices?
short: Orchestration has a coordinator directing steps; choreography lets services react to events without a central workflow controller.
answer: Orchestration makes state and compensation explicit. Choreography can reduce central coupling but becomes harder to reason about as the number of event interactions grows.
code:
Orchestrator -> A -> B -> C
Choreography: A event -> B event -> C
followups: Which is easier to observe?
When does choreography become difficult?
mistakes: Claiming one pattern is always superior.
interview: I choose based on workflow complexity. Explicit multi-step business processes often benefit from orchestration; simpler event reactions can work well with choreography.

title: How do you design idempotent state transitions?
short: A state transition should apply at most once for the same command or produce the same final state when repeated.
answer: Use a unique command ID, expected-version checks, conditional updates or business uniqueness constraints. Persist the processed command with the state change atomically when possible.
code: UPDATE orders SET status=PAID, version=version+1 WHERE id=? AND version=?
followups: How does optimistic locking help?
What if the client retries after a timeout?
mistakes: Checking state in one query and updating in a separate race-prone query.
interview: I make state transitions conditional and atomic using unique command IDs, version checks or database constraints.

title: What is optimistic concurrency control?
short: Optimistic concurrency assumes conflicts are uncommon and detects them at update time using a version or timestamp.
answer: The service reads version 5 and updates with a condition requiring version 5. If another writer changes it first, the update affects zero rows and the service handles the conflict.
code: UPDATE item SET qty=?, version=6 WHERE id=? AND version=5
followups: Optimistic vs pessimistic locking?
What should happen on conflict?
mistakes: Overwriting a newer value without checking version.
interview: Optimistic concurrency detects conflicting updates without holding database locks throughout the business operation.

title: What is a bulkhead for thread pools?
short: Separate thread pools or concurrency limits isolate slow workloads from each other.
answer: If payment calls consume a dedicated pool, a payment outage cannot occupy every worker needed by inventory or search. Pool sizes should be bounded and monitored.
followups: How do you size pools?
Virtual threads change what here?
mistakes: One shared unbounded executor for all remote calls.
interview: Thread-pool bulkheads isolate dependency pressure. They should be bounded and sized from measured workload and downstream capacity.

title: What is service-level objective (SLO) vs SLA?
short: An SLO is a target for service reliability; an SLA is a contractual commitment that may include consequences.
